summary: TRILL supports flow-level multipathing. This standards-track RFC defines a way to extend that to end stations connected to more than one edge RBridge, using a pseudo-nickname shared by the group, so traffic can use all attached links at once.

eli5.summary: If a house has two front doors, visitors can use either. A shared name lets the network treat both doors as one address.

questions: what is active-active access in trill
how does trill avoid mac address flip-flopping
subtitle: How a group of TRILL edge switches can share one virtual identity so a multiply connected end station can use all its links at once.

tldr.problem: When an end station is attached to several TRILL edge switches over an active-active link bundle, the switches see the same MAC address arrive from different places, duplicate or loop back multi-destination frames, and fail reverse-path checks.
tldr.mechanism: The edge switches act together as one virtual RBridge with a single pseudo-nickname used as the ingress nickname, elect a Designated Forwarder per VLAN, filter on ingress nickname, and share learned MAC addresses.
tldr.outcome: End stations can load-balance across all attached links while the rest of the campus sees a single stable ingress, without MAC address flip-flopping or duplicate frames.

today: RFC 7781 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. The alternative method for the same problem is described in RFC 7782.

sections.title: The Active-Active Access Problem
sections.content:
TRILL switches, called RBridges, forward frames using IS-IS link-state routing and a header with a Hop Count. In the base protocol only one edge RBridge per VLAN, the Appointed Forwarder, may serve end stations on a shared link, to avoid loops. But some end stations are connected to several edge RBridges at once through a Local Active-Active Link Protocol (LAALP) such as MC-LAG or DRNI, to gain bandwidth and reliability. All these uplinks should carry traffic for each VLAN.

Because an LAALP does not forward frames from one member port to another, member RBridges never see each other's Hellos. Each therefore believes it is the Appointed Forwarder for every VLAN on the link. The RFC lists the resulting problems, which are described in RFC 7379.

This document solves them by representing the group of edge RBridges as a virtual RBridge (RBv) with a pseudo-nickname. It notes that another method, RFC 7782, exists; both could be deployed for different groups in one campus, but the RFC says adopting just one method in a campus is desirable to reduce operating expense and troubleshooting complexity.
sections.eli5: Two doors into one house confuse the mail carrier, who keeps thinking the same person lives at two places. This RFC gives the house one shared address.

sections.title: The Virtual RBridge and Its Pseudo-Nickname
sections.content:
An RBv represents a group of edge RBridges to which at least one customer equipment (CE) node is multiply attached. More precisely it represents the ports on those RBridges that serve the CE over the LAALP, called RBv ports. An RBridge with one or more RBv ports is a member of that RBv.

The RBv is identified in the campus by its pseudo-nickname, different from any regular nickname. An RBv has one and only one. Each member advertises it in a Nickname sub-TLV in its TRILL IS-IS LSP, and SHOULD do so with the maximum priority of use, 0xFF, so a higher-priority RBridge cannot take it away. When a member loses its last RBv port it removes the pseudo-nickname from its LSP.

Members use the pseudo-nickname instead of their own nickname as the ingress nickname for frames received on RBv ports. A remote egress RBridge then sees one ingress for the same end station, whichever member forwarded the frame, so no flip-flopping appears. Frames from non-RBv ports still use the member's regular nickname.

An RBv is not a physical node, so pseudonode LSPs MUST NOT be created for it. It cannot be a distribution tree root: its tree root priority MUST be 0. To save nicknames, multiple CEs attached to exactly the same set of edge RBridges should share a single RBv.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the group signs letters with the same shared name. The people who receive them just see one sender and never get confused.

sections.title: Discovering Members and Choosing the Pseudo-Nickname
sections.content:
Edge RBridges find each other automatically. Each LAALP has an ID that is unique across the campus, such as the MC-LAG or DRNI System ID. Each edge RBridge advertises the IDs of its valid local LAALPs in E-L1FS FS-LSPs, and every LAALP-related RBridge collects them into a table of LAALP, OE-flag and set of edge RBridges.

An LAALP attached to only one RBridge is invalid. The valid ones are grouped by a fixed algorithm. First, every LAALP whose OE-flag is 1 (it wants to Occupy an RBv Exclusively) gets its own RBv. Then the remaining LAALPs are sorted by the number of RBridges in their sets, largest first, with ties broken by ascending LAALP ID. The first LAALP gets a new RBv, every other LAALP with exactly the same RBridge set joins it, and the process repeats until all are assigned.

In each RBv the member with the largest IS-IS System ID becomes the vDRB. It picks an available nickname following the usual TRILL rules and announces it in a PN-RBv APPsub-TLV. To limit disruption, the vDRB SHOULD try to reuse the pseudo-nickname the group used recently; members hint at it in their advertisements. The recommended choice is the available candidate reported by the most LAALPs, breaking ties by the smallest value.
sections.eli5: The doors that lead to exactly the same set of rooms are grouped together. Then the member with the biggest ID number gets to pick the group's shared name.

sections.title: Trees, Designated Forwarders and Ingress Filtering
sections.content:
Three problems affect multi-destination traffic, and each has its own fix.

Reverse path forwarding (RPF) failures. If different members ingress frames under the same pseudo-nickname onto the same distribution tree, some will arrive on unexpected ports and be dropped. The RFC adopts the Coordinated Multicast Trees approach of RFC 7783, where each member uses different trees and tells the campus via the Affinity sub-TLV.

Duplicates. Because every member thinks it is the Appointed Forwarder, a CE would get several copies. So one RBridge per VLAN is elected the Designated Forwarder (DF) for egressing multi-destination TRILL Data packets and for replicating local multi-destination frames to the CEs. It has no effect on unicast. Each member runs the same election: sort the RBridges by SHA-256 of the 6-byte System ID joined with the LAALP ID, number them from 0 to k-1, and for VLAN n choose the one numbered (n mod k).

Loopback. A multi-destination frame sent by a CE could be ingressed by one member and egressed back to the same CE by another. Ingress nickname filtering prevents this: if the ingress nickname matches the pseudo-nickname of the RBv on that port, the copy MUST NOT be egressed there. The check does not apply to regular access ports or to native frames replicated locally.
sections.eli5: To stop everyone from handing out the same flyer, one door-keeper per room is chosen using the same fair lottery on every switch. And a flyer is never handed back to the person who wrote it.

sections.title: Handling Frames and Packets
sections.content:
When a member ingresses a native frame, whether unicast or multi-destination, from an RBv port, it uses the RBv's pseudo-nickname as the ingress nickname. For multi-destination frames replicated locally to other RBv ports, ports on the same pseudo-nickname but a different LAALP only need the Appointed Forwarder check. Otherwise the DF check also applies. The learned MAC information SHOULD be shared with the other members.

For a unicast TRILL Data packet whose egress nickname is the local pseudo-nickname, the member learns the source MAC address and decapsulates the packet. It then uses the first applicable case: send to a local link, otherwise re-encapsulate to another member using that member's regular nickname as egress (increasing the Hop Count if it is too small to reach it), otherwise send out all local ports where it is Appointed Forwarder.

For multi-destination TRILL Data packets, on each RBv port where the RBridge is the Appointed Forwarder, both the DF check and the ingress nickname filtering check are made. The frame MUST NOT leave through a port that fails either.

On OAM, a member cannot use the pseudo-nickname as the ingress nickname when it originates OAM messages, because the responses might reach another member. It may use it in a response to an OAM message addressed to that pseudo-nickname. Since OAM messages are not used for MAC learning, this causes no flip-flopping.
sections.eli5: Mail addressed to the shared name goes to whichever door gets it. If that door is not the right one, it quietly passes the letter on to the member who can deliver it.

sections.title: MAC Synchronization, Link Failure and Consistency
sections.content:
A member may learn a MAC address that the returning traffic will need at another member, which would otherwise have to flood unknown unicast. So members SHOULD share what they learn. Address correspondences use MAC-Reachability (MAC-RI) sub-TLVs in ESADI-LSPs. MAC addresses learned from a specific LAALP are wrapped in a pair of boundary APPsub-TLVs, and the Topology-ID/Nickname field SHOULD carry the pseudo-nickname.

If a member's link to a CE fails, the member immediately removes its local MAC entry and installs one learned from another member of the LAALP. A unicast packet for the CE can then be re-encapsulated and tunnelled to that member, with the ingress nickname unchanged. Multi-destination packets need no special handling, since they reach all members of the new RBv.

The VLAN membership of all RBridge ports in an LAALP MUST be the same, and any VLAN to Fine-Grained Label mapping MUST be the same. TRILL switches MUST disable ports connected to an LAALP with inconsistent VLAN configuration. The OE-flag should not be asserted if any RBridge in the group does not implement it.
sections.eli5: If one door gets blocked, the members tell each other who was behind it so letters can be passed to a working door. All doors must also agree on which rooms exist.

sections.title: The New APPsub-TLVs
sections.content:
Four new sub-TLVs carry the information. Type values were allocated by IANA from the range below 255.

  • PN-LAALP-Membership (type 2) lists LAALP records. Each record has an OE bit, 7 reserved bits that MUST be zero, a Size byte, a 2-byte Reusing Pseudo-Nickname (zero if the LAALP is not served by an AAE group), and the LAALP ID. If OE values conflict between members, the flag is treated as 1.
  • PN-RBv (type 3) is sent by the vDRB. It carries the 2-byte pseudo-nickname, an LAALP ID Size byte and the LAALP IDs it serves. If Length is not 3 plus an integer multiple of the ID size, it is corrupt and MUST be ignored.
  • PN-MAC-RI-LAALP-INFO-START (type 4) and PN-MAC-RI-LAALP-INFO-END (type 5) enclose MAC-RI TLVs learned from one LAALP. A stray END is ignored, and the end of the ESADI-LSP closes an unmatched START.

An LAALP ID MUST be unique across the campus. A size of 8 bytes means an MC-LAG or DRNI identifier; other sizes are reserved for future documents. Recipients that are not LAALP-related ignore these sub-TLVs.
sections.eli5: These are four little labelled notes the switches pass around so they can agree on groups, names and who knows which addresses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authenticity of content in IS-IS PDUs relies on the regular IS-IS mechanisms, and ESADI extensions follow RFC 7357. General TRILL security considerations are in RFC 6325.

Deployed LAALPs are proprietary, so security over group membership is also proprietary. If authentication is not used, a rogue RBridge that joins an active-active edge group can disrupt traffic. With N RBridges in the group it could typically control 1/Nth of the traffic flowing out and a similar amount of unicast traffic flowing in. For multi-destination traffic it could control all that is in a VLAN for which it is the DF, and it can exercise substantial control over the DF election by changing its own System ID.
sections.eli5: If a stranger sneaks into the group of doors, they can steal some of the mail that passes through, so the group should check who joins.

items.title: MAC flip-flopping
items.text: Remote switches learn the same MAC address behind different ingress nicknames, causing reordering.

items.title: Duplicate egress
items.text: Several members egress the same multi-destination frame to the CE.

items.title: Loopback
items.text: A frame ingressed by one member is egressed back to its sender by another.

items.title: RPF check failures
items.text: Frames from different members on one tree arrive on unexpected ports and are dropped.
